title: Build your little world
subtitle: Bring everything together, one small step at a time.

lessons.title: 01 / Sculpt your planet
lessons.concept: A capstone in five small steps
body: You now have the pieces to build a miniature world. Each capstone step starts from a working scene, so you can focus on one decision at a time.

Our planet uses an icosahedron with two levels of subdivision and flat shading. It gives a faceted, illustrated feel at a modest triangle count. Make it your own with a warm coral surface. The moon is a child of an orbit group, ready for animation later.
lessons.task: Change the planet material color to #edaa91.
lessons.hint: Use planet.material.color.set on the last line.

quiz.question: What makes the planet appear faceted?
quiz.explanation: Flat shading uses distinct triangle normals to show the individual faces.

lessons.title: 02 / Add an orbital ring
body: A ring gives the scene a strong silhouette and a visual contrast to the round planet. Its tilt makes the composition readable from our camera angle.

The ring is a torus with a very thin tube. It exists in the scene but starts hidden. Reveal it, then experiment with its rotation after finishing the check. Visibility is useful for optional details; it does not dispose their resources.
lessons.hint: The geometry and material are already in place.

quiz.question: Setting visible to false…
options: Keeps the object but skips its display
quiz.explanation: Visibility is separate from scene membership and resource lifetime.

lessons.title: 03 / Set the moon in motion
body: The moon’s local X position is its orbital radius. Rotating the parent group moves the moon around the origin while leaving that local offset intact.

This combines scene hierarchy, radians, and delta time. Spin the orbit at a gentle speed and independently rotate the planet. A real astronomical simulation would need a different scale and motion model; this is a playful visual composition.
lessons.hint: The callback rotates orbit, not moon. That keeps the radius fixed.

quiz.question: Why rotate the moon’s parent group?
options: To orbit while preserving its local offset
quiz.explanation: The parent’s rotation transforms the child’s position around the group origin.

lessons.title: 04 / A sky full of points
lessons.concept: Background depth without hundreds of meshes
body: Our stars use one Points object with a shared material. Their positions lie on a sphere around the scene, which gives depth as you orbit the camera.

The deterministic pattern keeps every run consistent. Their size is small enough to read as distant points. Add the field by enabling its visibility, then compare the scene with and without this final layer of context.

quiz.question: Why use one Points object for these stars?
options: Each star needs a separate mesh
It batches many simple points efficiently
Points remove the need for a scene
quiz.explanation: A point cloud avoids a separate mesh and draw call for each small star.

lessons.title: 05 / The final look
lessons.concept: Tone mapping and a finished scene
body: Tone mapping compresses a wide range of scene brightness into what a display can show. ACESFilmicToneMapping gives highlights a softer rolloff; exposure then adjusts the overall brightness before that mapping.

Enable it and take a look around your finished world. You have worked with space, geometry, cameras, materials, light, textures, time, interaction, assets, and shaders. Export this scene from the editor to keep building in your own project. The workspace API is documented alongside the exported code.
lessons.hint: Keep toneMappingExposure at 1.2. You can tune it after the lesson.

quiz.question: Tone mapping mainly helps map…
options: Scene brightness into the display range
quiz.explanation: Tone mapping controls how scene brightness is represented on a display.
